title: Cities in a County Finder: Full Settlement List
description: List every city, town and village in a US county with the Cities in a County Finder — from the county's mapped boundary, CSV included. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a large Texas county returns dozens of settlements — cities, towns and villages with coordinates — including the unincorporated places mailing lists usually miss.
quick_answer: The Cities in a County Finder takes a county name and state and returns its full settlement list from the county's OpenStreetMap boundary: cities, towns and villages with their coordinates, downloadable as CSV. Type the county, add the two-letter state code, and read the county as its people populate it.
steps_intro: Counties contain more places than their famous city. List them all:

body.t: Coverage claims get audited against complete lists. A county 'fully covered' means these places, each one — context from
The village an ancestor's record names may not be the county seat — the full list is where small places are findable at all.
Settlements with coordinates are a market's skeleton: plot them and the county's real shape replaces its outline.
Every settlement is somewhere people must be reached. Complete lists are the difference between coverage and a story about coverage.

examples.label: Example · Why the state code matters

body.t: Dozens of counties share names across states — there is a Washington County in most of them. County plus state code is the unique key; the finder asks for both on purpose.
In rural counties most named places are unincorporated communities. A list built from mapped settlements catches them; a list of incorporated cities alone would call the county emptier than it is.

faq: Does it include unincorporated places?
Yes — settlements as mapped: cities, towns and villages including unincorporated communities with a mapped point. That completeness is the page's purpose.
Why add the state?
County names repeat across America. The state code makes the county unique; without it the finder would be guessing among namesakes.
Can I use the tool without sharing my precise location?
Yes — you type a county; your location is irrelevant to it.
Why might a boundary or place name look different elsewhere?
OpenStreetMap's county boundary and settlement tags evolve with mapper contributions; another source may draw a line or spell a name differently.
Does MapBench store my browser location?
No — and this tool never asks for it.
A settlement is missing.
Likely unmapped or mapped without a place point yet. Open data's gaps are visible and fixable by mappers — the list shows what the map knows today.
Can I get places within a radius instead?
That is Cities Within a Drawn Area and the radius family — a circle's list rather than a county's. Different boundary, different question.
The list is huge — biggest counties?
Large western counties and big urban ones hold dozens of settlements. The CSV exists because some lists outgrow the screen honestly.
Are ghost towns listed?
If mapped as a place, a historic settlement can appear tagged as it is recorded. The map's memory is long; check the type field.
Can I list places in a parish or borough?
County-equivalents in Census geography behave the same for listing purposes where the boundary data exists.
Why does a suburb appear in two counties' lists?
It should not — a point falls in one. If it does, one list's boundary generalised across it. The county lookup's polygon test arbitrates.
